decompositions.name: triage the TA inbox
decompositions.yaml:
name: triage the TA inbox
messages:
- role: user
  content: 'Triage the inbox: a one-line gist for every message, and for any message that
    contains code, also a correctness check.'
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    I don't know which messages contain code — let the model infer it. Classify every
    message in ONE parallel `llm.batch` call (structured {gist, has_code} per item, cheap
    tier), then review the flagged ones in ONE parallel `code_reviewer.batch` call (coder
    tier). Batching both keeps the calls concurrent instead of looping per message.
    </think>
    <repl>
    from pydantic import BaseModel

    class Triaged(BaseModel):
        gist: str
        has_code: bool          # the message contains a code snippet, not just prose

    # 1. Classify every message in parallel (one batched llm call, cheap tier).
    classify_prompts = [f"Give a one-line gist and whether this message contains code:\n{m['text']}"
                        for m in inbox]
    triaged = llm.batch(classify_prompts, schema=Triaged)

    # 2. Review only the flagged code messages, in parallel (one batched code_reviewer call).
    code = [m for m, t in zip(inbox, triaged) if t.has_code]
    code_reviews = code_reviewer.batch([m["text"] for m in code])

    # 3. Organize the results into plain dicts, keyed by message id.
    gists = {m["id"]: t.gist for m, t in zip(inbox, triaged)}
    reviews = {m["id"]: review for m, review in zip(code, code_reviews)}

    FinalAnswer({"gists": gists, "reviews": reviews})
    </repl>

It's completely normal to feel stressed, so be kind to yourself as you navigate these final exams. Here are some friendly reminders to help you stay on track and keep stress at bay:

items.value:
You are the experience manager. Your procedure is fixed and you run all four steps for
EVERY task, however easy it looks — what this agent is for is the record it leaves behind,
not the shortest path to one answer:
  1. RECALL  — `hits = rag.search(task, k=1)`, the closest lesson from past runs.
  2. DELEGATE — `solver = subagent(namespace="solver")` with NO task, so you keep the
     sub-agent, then `answer = solver(task + the recalled lesson as a hint)`. You never
     solve the task yourself.
  3. ASK HOW — `method = solver("How did you solve that? ...")`. Put it to the SAME solver:
     it still has the solve in its context, and the lesson has to be its account of its own
     method, not your guess at it.
  4. REMEMBER — `rag.add([...])` with `method` as the lesson text, then `solver.close()`
     and `FinalAnswer(answer)`.
`rag`, `subagent` and `FinalAnswer` are already bound in your REPL — never import them.

decompositions.name: recall, delegate, ask how, then remember
decompositions.yaml:
name: recall, delegate, ask how, then remember
messages:
- role: user
  content: 'Solve and remember: What is 12 miles in kilometers?'
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    Before solving, recall the most relevant lesson from memory so I can hand the
    solver a proven approach instead of making it rediscover one.
    </think>
    <repl>
    task = "What is 12 miles in kilometers?"
    hits = rag.search(task, k=1)
    print(hits[0]["id"], "||", hits[0]["text"])
    </repl>
- role: user
  content: |
    <observation>
    mem-miles-to-km || Task type: convert a distance in miles to kilometers.
    Lesson: multiply the number of miles by 1.60934, round to 2 decimals, and answer "<x> km".
    </observation>
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    A matching lesson. Delegate to the solver with it as a hint. I will want to ask the
    solver afterwards how it solved the task, so I HOLD the sub-agent instead of using the
    one-shot form: subagent(namespace="solver") with no task returns the agent itself, and
    calling it drives one task while keeping the conversation for the next one.
    </think>
    <repl>
    solver = subagent(namespace="solver")
    answer = solver(f"{task}\n\nHint from past experience:\n{hits[0]['text']}")
    print(answer)
    </repl>
- role: user
  content: |
    <observation>
    12 miles is 19.31 km.
    </observation>
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    Now ask that same solver how it got there. The lesson has to be the solver's account of
    its own method, and it has to be stated for any task of this kind rather than for these
    numbers, or nothing will ever retrieve it again.
    </think>
    <repl>
    method = solver(
        "How did you solve that? Reply with the reusable method only, two lines:\n"
        "line 1: 'Task type: <the general kind of task>'\n"
        "line 2: 'Lesson: <the steps, stated for any input of that kind>'\n"
        "Do not mention the specific numbers from this task."
    )
    print(method)
    </repl>
- role: user
  content: |
    <observation>
    Task type: convert a distance in miles to kilometers.
    Lesson: multiply the number of miles by 1.60934, round to 2 decimals, and answer "<x> km".
    </observation>
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    That is the lesson, in the solver's words. Store it, release the solver I was holding
    (the one-shot form closes the child for you; this form leaves it to me), and answer.
    </think>
    <repl>
    rag.add([{"id": "mem-run-miles-12",
              "text": method,
              "metadata": {"kind": "memory", "skill": "unit-conversion"}}])
    solver.close()
    FinalAnswer(answer)
    </repl>

asked afterwards how you solved it, that is a question about the task you just did: answer

decompositions.name: parse a drug label into the graph
decompositions.yaml:
name: parse a drug label into the graph
messages:
- role: user
  content: |
    Add to the graph (document id `label`): "Acetaminophen treats fever and pain. Warfarin interacts with ibuprofen."
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    Inspect the schema first, so I reuse existing models or know to define new ones
    before parsing.
    </think>
    <repl>
    print(kg.schema_description())
    </repl>
- role: user
  content: |
    <observation>
    No models registered yet.
    </observation>
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    Nothing registered yet. Define Treats(drug, condition) and Interacts(a, b) —
    drug names are EntityRefs so they stay linkable. Register the source document,
    then let llm_parser (which already knows the extraction task) pull typed facts.
    </think>
    <repl>
    class Treats(kg.KGModel):
        drug: kg.EntityRef
        condition: str
    class Interacts(kg.KGModel):
        a: kg.EntityRef
        b: kg.EntityRef
    label = "Acetaminophen treats fever and pain. Warfarin interacts with ibuprofen."
    kg.add_doc("label", text=label)
    facts = llm_parser(label, schema=list[Treats | Interacts])
    print(facts)
    </repl>
- role: user
  content: |
    <observation>
    [Treats(drug='Acetaminophen', condition='fever'), Treats(drug='Acetaminophen', condition='pain'), Interacts(a='Warfarin', b='ibuprofen')]
    </observation>
- role: assistant
  content: |
    <think>
    Add each fact with a provenance span locating its evidence in the label, so
    explanations can cite the source text later.
    </think>
    <repl>
    for f in facts:
        key = f.condition if isinstance(f, Treats) else f.b
        span = kg.quote(label, key, doc_id="label")
        kg.add_fact(f, source=kg.Provenance("stated on the label", source=span))
    FinalAnswer(f"Added {len(facts)} facts from the label.")
    </repl>

tools.name: llm
tools.description: Single LLM call: llm(prompt) -> str. Concurrent batch: llm.batch([prompt1, prompt2, ...]) -> list[str]. Use for language tasks on data you already hold (summarise, extract, classify, rewrite).

tools.name: rag
tools.description: In-memory semantic retrieval store. rag.search(query, collection='default', k=5, where=None) -> list of {id, text, metadata, distance} nearest first; pass where={'namespace': ...} to filter on metadata. rag.add(docs, collection='default') indexes a list of {'id': ..., 'text': ..., 'metadata': {...}} dicts, growing the store for the rest of the run. Configured corpora are preloaded into 'default'.

tools.name: kg
tools.description:
Symbolic knowledge graph (Clingo ASP) with namespaces, provenance and semantic
search. A thin façade over `Facts` (clingo), `Docs` (files), and `Search` (RagStore);
pass a `deep_reasoner.tools.rag.RagStore` to enable `search`. This docstring is the
tool's agent-facing API — it is what the `kg` binding shows the agent by default.

Inspect the schema BEFORE you query or add — the models are not fixed:
  - kg.schema_description() -> a text summary of the models that exist.
  - kg.models() -> {name: class}; kg.model('Name') -> one class (rebuilt from a loaded
    graph too). Reuse a class as a query pattern or an llm(schema=...) output type, or
    subclass kg.KGModel for a new relation.

Define models and add data:
  - class Thing(kg.KGModel): ...   # free vars kg.V('X') are allowed in any field.
  - kg.add_fact(inst, namespace=, source=kg.Provenance('note', source=...))  # a fact.
  - kg.add_rule(kg.Rule(when=<body>, then=<head>))   # a derivation rule; bodies use
    kg.And / kg.Or / kg.Not + comparisons.
  - kg.add_doc(id, text=)          # a document, for quote/search provenance.
  - kg.add_raw_rule(asp)           # full-clingo escape hatch (aggregates, constraints).

Query and explain:
  - kg.query(target, namespaces=)  # model type/pattern -> list[Model]; ground -> bool;
    And/Or/Not -> list[dict]. Put kg.V('X') in the fields you want back, e.g.
    Cls = kg.model('Prereq'); kg.query(Cls(course='CS450', needs=kg.V('N'))).
  - kg.explain(fact)               # a readable numbered proof (struct=True -> Derivation).
  - kg.search(query, scope='facts'|'documents'|'both', model=, namespaces=)
                                   # -> list[(item, score)] semantic search.

Entity identity (owl:sameAs): use kg.EntityRef for identity fields, then
  - kg.enable_link_propagation() and kg.add_fact(kg.Linked(a=, b=))  # every fact,
    deduction AND query about one identifier also holds for the other.
  - kg.search_entities(text)       # similar known entity ids to inspect before linking.

tools.name: safe_url
tools.description: Namespace-gated URL fetcher. safe_url.set_allowlist([host, ...]) -> a new configured tool (only in a configuring namespace); pass that configured tool to a sub-agent via subagent(..., tools={'safe_url': configured}). safe_url.fetch(url) -> str fetches a URL whose host is on the allow-list (only in a calling namespace). Denials raise PermissionError.

tools.name: claude_code
tools.description: Delegate a task to a Claude Code run: claude(task) -> ClaudeResult (str(result) is its answer, or why it failed). claude.batch([t1, t2, ...]) runs many concurrently, one forked worker each. schema=<pydantic model> returns a validated object. claude.fork(**overrides) gives a session that keeps its own context across turns and has its own working directory. If the task has a decision nobody has made, it stops and asks instead of guessing; answer by sending the decision back into the same session (send + anext), not by starting a new one. IT IS A SEPARATE PROCESS AND SHARES NO VARIABLES WITH THIS REPL: interpolate small values into the task string, and pass anything large as a PATH it can read.

tools.name: code_reviewer
tools.description: Single LLM call: llm(prompt) -> str. Concurrent batch: llm.batch([prompt1, prompt2, ...]) -> list[str]. Use for language tasks on data you already hold (summarise, extract, classify, rewrite).
tools.config:
code_reviewer:
  factory: llm
  model: coder
  system_prompt: |
    You are a terse code reviewer. Given a short Python snippet and the question about it,
    name the bug in one sentence, then give the one-line fix. No preamble.

tools.name: llm_parser
tools.description: Single LLM call: llm(prompt) -> str. Concurrent batch: llm.batch([prompt1, prompt2, ...]) -> list[str]. Use for language tasks on data you already hold (summarise, extract, classify, rewrite).
tools.config:
llm_parser:
  factory: llm
  system_prompt: |
    You extract structured facts from a short text into the schema you are
    given. Return ONLY facts explicitly stated in the text, matching the schema
    exactly — do not infer, expand, or invent, and keep names exactly as written.

tools.name: waitlist
tools.description:
Course waitlists that survive the run.

waitlist.join(student, course) -> str   "enrolled", or "waitlisted at N"
waitlist.of(course)            -> list[str]  everyone queued, in joining order
waitlist.enrolled(course)      -> list[str]  the ones who got a seat

`PersistentTool` is the contract the run's end-of-run hook uses: a `persist_dir`
and a `save()` taking no arguments. Inheriting it is the explicit way to say so;
having both members is the other.
tools.config:
waitlist:
  factory: build_waitlist
  factory_from: ./tools.py
  capacity: 2
